---Role---

You are a helpful assistant responding to questions about data in the reports provided.

---Goal---

Generate a response of the target length and format that responds to the user's question, summarizing all information in the input reports appropriate for the response length and format, and incorporating any relevant general knowledge while being as specific, accurate and concise as possible.

If you don't know the answer, just say so. Do not make anything up.

Points supported by data should list their data references as follows:

"This is an example sentence supported by multiple data references [Data: <dataset name> (record ids); <dataset name> (record ids)]."

Do not list more than 5 record ids in a single reference. Instead, list the top 5 most relevant record ids and add "+more" to indicate that there are more.

For example:

"Person X is the owner of Company Y and subject to many allegations of wrongdoing [Data: Sources (1, 5, 15)]."

Do not include information where the supporting evidence for it is not provided.

If you decide to use general knowledge, you should add a delimiter stating that the information is not supported by the data tables. For example:

"Person X is the owner of Company Y and subject to many allegations of wrongdoing. [Data: General Knowledge (href)]"

---Data Reports---

['# Redirect Authentication Decision\n\nThe supplied evidence places the decision in `rebuild_auth`, which reconstructs authentication during a redirect. When the redirected request already has an `Authorization` header, `rebuild_auth` calls `should_strip_auth` with the original URL and the destination URL [Data: Entities (789); Relationships (1056)]. If that decision is true, the existing header is removed before the redirected request continues. Thus, the direct trace is: redirect processing invokes `rebuild_auth`; `rebuild_auth` compares the two URLs through `should_strip_auth`; a true result causes the `Authorization` header to be stripped.\n\nThe strongest explicitly supported trigger is a host change. The test for `http://example.com/foo` to `http://another.example.com/` asserts that `should_strip_auth` returns true [Data: Entities (1290); Relationships (2110)]. Authentication is also stripped for an HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade and for a change involving non-equivalent ports, such as `http://example.com:1234/foo` to `https://example.com:4321/bar` [Data: Entities (1291, 1294); Relationships (2111, 2136)]. The policy is differentiated rather than stripping on every scheme change: an HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade can retain authentication for equivalent standard ports, and equivalent default-port cases are asserted not to strip [Data: Entities (1292, 1295); Relationships (2112, 2138)].\n\nAfter the old header is removed, the environment-based replacement condition is that trusted-environment handling is enabled and netrc lookup supplies new credentials. The summary describes `rebuild_auth` as potentially reapplying netrc credentials under trusted environment settings, using `prepared_request.prepare_auth(new_auth)` when new credentials are available [Data: Entities (789); Relationships (1066)]. In operational terms supported by the snapshot, replacement therefore requires `trust_env` to permit environment credential lookup and a nonempty netrc result (`new_auth`); the new credentials are then passed to `prepare_auth`.\n\nImportant uncertainty remains. The supplied records do not expose the `Session` implementation, the runtime binding of `should_strip_auth`, the exact netrc lookup code, or the concrete definition of `trust_env`. They establish tested behavior and documented call relationships, not independently verified production execution. The evidence also does not show what happens when netrc lookup returns no credentials beyond indicating that replacement requires credentials to be available.\n', 'In `src/requests/sessions.py`, inside `rebuild_auth`, the netrc lookup is controlled by the exact conditional expression `get_netrc_auth(url) if self.trust_env else None`. Therefore, `get_netrc_auth(url)` is called only when `self.trust_env` is truthy; otherwise, `new_auth` is set to `None`. [Data: Sources (53); Entities (789, 762)]\n\nIf the lookup returns credentials (`new_auth is not None`), the code replaces or reapplies authentication with `prepared_request.prepare_auth(new_auth)`. The supplied snapshot does not show the definition of `get_netrc_auth` or establish whether `self.trust_env` is enabled by default. [Data: Sources (53); Entities (762)]', 'The supplied evidence does not show a single test that explicitly combines a cross-host redirect, stripping an `Authorization` header, and then replacing it with netrc credentials.\n\nThe netrc credential behavior is verified by `test_basicauth_with_netrc` in `tests/test_requests.py` (the supplied excerpt is at `tests/test_requests.py:L640-L786`). It temporarily replaces `requests.sessions.get_netrc_auth`, confirms that the returned netrc credentials succeed, and confirms that explicitly supplied wrong credentials override netrc credentials and receive HTTP 401. [Data: Sources (85); Entities (1151, 1160, 1159)]\n\nThe header-stripping behavior is covered separately by `test_should_strip_auth_host_change`, which expects stripping when the host changes, and `test_auth_is_retrained_for_redirect_on_host` is not present; the supplied entity is actually `test_auth_is_retained_for_redirect_on_host`, which verifies that same-host redirects retain `Authorization`. `test_auth_is_stripped_on_http_downgrade` verifies removal on an HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect. [Data: Entities (1290, 1289, 1288)]\n\nThe implementation path is described by `rebuild_auth`: it removes `Authorization` when `should_strip_auth(...)` is true, then obtains netrc credentials and applies them when trusted environment settings permit. Thus, the snapshot supports the implementation condition and the related tests, but is insufficient to identify a test proving the complete cross-host strip-and-netrc-replacement sequence. [Data: Entities (789, 762)]', '`get_netrc_auth` is defined in `src/requests/utils.py` within the supplied `L170-L320` snapshot. It first checks `os.environ.get("NETRC")`. If that variable is set, it searches only the specified path; otherwise, it searches the default locations `~/.netrc` and `~/_netrc` via the `NETRC_FILES` constant. Each candidate is passed to `os.path.expanduser`, and the first existing path is selected. If expansion fails because `$HOME` cannot be resolved, or if no candidate exists, the function returns without credentials. [Data: Sources (62); Entities (898, 860)]\n\nAfter selecting a file, the function parses the URL with `urlparse`, removes the port from the URL\'s network location, and uses the resulting host name to query `netrc(netrc_path).authenticators(host)`. When credentials are found, it returns a `(login, password)` tuple. If the netrc entry has no login, it uses the alternate login field indicated by the parsed authenticator tuple. [Data: Sources (62); Relationships (1277, 1290)]\n\nThe function skips netrc authentication when parsing or reading fails with `NetrcParseError` or `OSError`; it re-raises those exceptions only when `raise_errors=True`. Import-related `ImportError` and `AttributeError` cases are also caught. The supplied snapshot shows the calls to Python\'s external `netrc` parser but does not include that parser\'s implementation. [Data: Sources (62); Entities (886, 902)]', 'No supplied source test explicitly follows a cross-host redirect and checks that netrc credentials are reapplied. The closest evidence is `test_basicauth_with_netrc` in the test suite, which temporarily replaces `requests.sessions.get_netrc_auth`, verifies netrc credentials, checks that explicit wrong credentials return status 401, and restores the original callable; the snapshot does not show a cross-host redirect in this test [Data: Entities (1151); Relationships (1770)].\n\nThe available implementation evidence shows that `get_netrc_auth(url)` can obtain credentials for a redirected URL when environment trust is enabled, but the relevant redirect decision and condition are not shown in the supplied test source [Data: Entities (762); Sources (62)].']

### Decision Trace

During redirect processing, `rebuild_auth` in `src/requests/sessions.py` compares the original and destination URLs by calling `should_strip_auth`. If that function returns `True`, `rebuild_auth` removes the existing `Authorization` header before continuing the redirected request [Data: Entities (789); Relationships (1056)].

A cross-host redirect is an explicitly supported trigger: the change from `http://example.com/foo` to `http://another.example.com/` makes `should_strip_auth` return `True`, so the header is stripped. The policy also strips authentication for HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrades and non-equivalent port changes, but does not strip it for every scheme change; equivalent HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrades and default-port cases may retain authentication [Data: Entities (1290, 1291, 1292, 1294, 1295); Relationships (2110, 2111, 2112, 2136, 2138)].

### Environment Replacement

After stripping the header, `rebuild_auth` evaluates the exact condition `get_netrc_auth(url) if self.trust_env else None`. Therefore, `get_netrc_auth(url)` is consulted only when `self.trust_env` is truthy. If it returns credentials (`new_auth is not None`), `rebuild_auth` reapplies authentication through `prepared_request.prepare_auth(new_auth)` [Data: Sources (53); Entities (789, 762); Relationships (1066)].

`get_netrc_auth` is defined in `src/requests/utils.py` within the supplied `L170-L320` snapshot. It searches the `NETRC` path when that environment variable is set, or otherwise checks the default `~/.netrc` and `~/_netrc` locations, then looks up credentials for the redirected URL's host [Data: Sources (62); Entities (898, 860); Relationships (1277, 1290)]. Missing files, unresolved paths, parsing failures, or unavailable credentials result in no replacement under the supplied evidence; exceptions may be suppressed unless `raise_errors=True` [Data: Sources (62); Entities (886, 902)].

### Evidence Limitation

The supplied tests verify host-change stripping and netrc authentication separately, but do not show a single test that follows a cross-host redirect, confirms header removal, and confirms netrc credentials are reapplied afterward. The evidence establishes the implementation path and conditions, but does not establish the runtime default value of `self.trust_env` or a complete end-to-end test of that sequence [Data: Entities (1151, 1290, 1289, 1288); Relationships (1770)].
